extracted.intended_audience: poets, dramatists, literary critics, and educated readers interested in aesthetics and craft of drama and poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Critical-aesthetic criteria for judging and composing drama and poetry, with emphasis on plot construction, character-formation, diction, translation fidelity, and the balance between the ideal (generic) and the individual (specific).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sweep of long cadences over single-line vigour
rubrics_metrics.description: Preference for 'cadences, and the sweep of whole paragraphs' and 'linked sweetness long drawn out' rather than the 'even flow' or prominence of antithetic, single-line vigour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single, antithetic lines are injurious to the total effect except when introduced for some specific purpose; favour extended rhythmic movement and the cumulative effect of linked passages for larger poetic works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fidelity and accuracy in translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Translations should not add or omit material; bad translations may contain 'pages on pages not in the original' or lack half the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inserting material not in the source or omitting substantial portions; aim for fidelity to the original's content and spirit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect language-specific idiom and economy
rubrics_metrics.description: Different languages have distinct capacities for concentration and line-equivalence (e.g., 'a German line proved always sufficient for a Greek or Latin one' while English often needs more space).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force line-for-line equivalence across languages; observe each language's idiom, rhythmic norms, and syllabic economy when translating or composing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful structural planning (the plan of odes/poems)
rubrics_metrics.description: Importance of a well-devised plan: Klopstock 'values himself upon the plan of his odes' and accuses modern lyrical writers of gross deficiency in this respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Devote time to an overall plan or structure for long poems and odes; avoid producing lyric material without architectural coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet's role: elevate rather than pander
rubrics_metrics.description: It is 'the province of a great poet to raise people up to his own level, not to descend to theirs.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to elevate the audience's taste and understanding; avoid cheap or pandering devices intended merely to please current popular appetite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid corrupting native idiom by excessive borrowing
rubrics_metrics.description: Borrowing idioms from another tongue is 'a very dangerous practice'; Milton sometimes injured his prose and verse by this liberty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer native linguistic resources; use foreign idioms sparingly and only where they genuinely serve the work's diction and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use native prose/poetic models for purity
rubrics_metrics.description: Dryden's prose is recommended 'as models of pure and native English.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study exemplary native models to cultivate purity of diction and idiom appropriate to your language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot construction, sentiment, morals, and diction in drama (Lessing's standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessing's dramas are praised for 'the construction of the plot; the good sense of the sentiments; the sobriety of the morals; and the high polish of the diction and dialogue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drama on plot architecture, truth and sensibility of sentiments, moral sobriety (avoiding corrupt or bizarre moral postures), and refined, polished dialogue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth and imagination vs. polished construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Lessing's deficiency is 'in depth and imagination' even as his excellence is construction and polish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance formal construction with imaginative depth; a well-made plot should not substitute for imaginative richness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid extravagant affectation and melodramatic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Schiller’s ROBBERS was criticized for extravagance and later affectations (studied feebleness, metrical affectation, pedantry of chorus); German romantic drama often employed 'horrific incidents... ruined castles, dungeons, trap-doors, skeletons, ... perpetual moonshine.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of sensational Gothic tropes and theatrical extravagance used merely to shock; prefer credible dramatic means over cheap sensationalism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of bloated style and over-sensibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Compositions that mix 'the bloated style and peculiar rhythm of Hervey', 'figurative metaphysics and solemn epigrams of Young', and Richardson's 'loaded sensibility' produce a sickly effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid inflated, prosaic-poetic rhythms, overwrought metaphysics, and an indulgent, minute sensibility that substitutes feeling for form and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of borrowed material and common mythology
rubrics_metrics.description: Wieland's 'thefts' are defensible because 'books and fables of old romance writers' are treated as a sort of common property; a man is free to take from them what he can make good use of.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using material from shared mythic or romantic sources is acceptable when transformed skillfully; acknowledge imitation by improving or reconfiguring inherited material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal art: balance of the generic and the individual
rubrics_metrics.description: The ideal consists 'in the happy balance of the generic with the individual'—the generic makes a character representative and instructive while the individual gives it living interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose characters that combine symbolic/representative traits with distinct, individuating detail; avoid figures that are purely abstract or purely portrait-like.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain dramatic probability by internal harmony
rubrics_metrics.description: A poet may secure 'dramatic probability, sufficient for dramatic pleasure, even when the component characters and incidents border on impossibility' if 'the whole of his work be in harmony.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve consistent internal laws (tone, character logic, thematic unity) so that improbable events or supernatural elements remain acceptable to the reader/audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create intelligible idealized characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Even highly idealized or abstract characters (e.g., Don Juan or Milton's Satan) must be 'intelligible'—their construction must make them believable within the poet's terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that idealized figures are coherent and psychologically or symbolically comprehensible so the audience can grant negative faith in their existence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid cheap sentimentalism (manufactured tears)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deluging an audience with tears is 'nothing more easy' and 'is done every day by the meanest writers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not manufacture pathetic effects by mechanical devices; instead seek genuine moral and imaginative causes for emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power as necessary vehicle for virtue and interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Without power, virtue is 'insufficient and incapable of revealing its being'; coexistence of intellectual power with guilt heightens dramatic interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant protagonists sufficient power (social, intellectual, physical) so their virtues or vices are manifest and consequential; juxtapose power and moral failure when aiming for compelling tragedy or character-interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poet solicits a willing suspension of disbelief, not credulity
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet asks for 'that sort of negative faith... that we yield ourselves to a dream... only, not to disbelieve.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arrange your work to invite the reader to suspend disbelief through coherence and aesthetic authority, rather than by demanding literal belief in impossible events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of distance and idealization to mitigate moral shock
rubrics_metrics.description: Extravagance and 'super-human entireness' of a character can prevent wickedness from shocking the reader by placing it at a safe imaginative remove.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When representing extreme vice, consider idealization or distance (mythic scale, symbolic treatment) to allow aesthetic appreciation without overwhelming moral revulsion.
